title: Explain the principles of business and the role of information technology

lessons.title: Principles of business in the export environment
lessons.html:
What a business is

A business combines resources to produce goods or services that customers value, with the aim of earning a profit and surviving over time. In the perishable produce export chain, businesses include farms, packhouses, cold stores, transport companies, exporters and service providers.

Core principles

  • Customer value: a business survives only if customers are willing to pay more than it costs to produce what they want. For exporters, value means the right fruit, in the right condition, at the right time.
  • Profitability and cash flow: income must exceed costs over time, and cash must be available to pay bills when due. Seasonal businesses must manage the gap between spending on inputs and receiving payment from markets.
  • Efficient use of resources: land, water, labour, capital and information must be used productively.
  • Risk management: weather, markets, exchange rates and regulations create risks that must be identified and managed.
  • Legal and ethical compliance: businesses operate within company, tax, labour, safety, environmental and export law, and are increasingly judged on ethics and sustainability.
  • Stakeholders: owners, employees, customers, suppliers, communities and government all have interests in the business.

Business functions

FunctionRole in an export packhouse
General managementStrategy, planning, coordination
OperationsReceiving, packing, cooling and dispatch
Marketing and salesRelationships with exporters and buyers, programmes
FinanceBudgets, costing, payments, reporting
Human resourcesRecruitment, training, labour relations
Purchasing and logisticsPackaging, chemicals, transport bookings
Quality and complianceStandards, audits, certification

Forms of ownership

Sole proprietors, partnerships, private and public companies registered with CIPC, co-operatives and state-owned entities each differ in liability, ownership, tax and control. Many packhouses are companies or co-operatives owned by groups of growers.

The business environment

Managers must scan the micro environment (internal resources), the market environment (customers, suppliers, competitors) and the macro environment (economic, political, social, technological, legal and ecological factors). Tools such as SWOT analysis help summarise strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats.

lessons.title: The role of information technology
lessons.html:
Why IT matters in perishable exports

The export chain moves fast and depends on accurate information. A container cannot be loaded without correct pallet data, and an exporter cannot sell fruit it cannot see in stock. Information technology (IT) supports every business function.

Common IT applications

  • Traceability and pallet systems: barcodes or QR codes on bins, cartons and pallets, scanned at each step, linking product to orchard, packing run and container.
  • Packhouse management software: intake, packout reports per grower, stock in cold store, dispatch.
  • Quality systems: tablets for QC sampling with results uploaded instantly, photos of defects, dashboards of pass rates.
  • Cold chain monitoring: wireless sensors in cold rooms with alarms sent to cellphones; data loggers and remote container monitoring.
  • Electronic certification and bookings: online inspection requests, electronic certificates and shipping bookings.
  • Accounting and payroll: invoicing, cost tracking, grower payments, wages and tax submissions.
  • Communication: email, messaging and video calls with overseas buyers.
  • Farm management: spray records, irrigation scheduling, yield estimates, satellite or drone imagery.

Benefits

  • Faster, more accurate information and fewer manual errors.
  • Real-time visibility of stock, quality and temperatures.
  • Better decisions using reports and trends.
  • Easier compliance and audit evidence.

Risks and controls

  • System failure and power outages: keep back-ups, uninterruptible power and manual fall-back procedures.
  • Data loss: regular, tested back-ups, stored off site or in the cloud.
  • Cyber security: strong passwords, updates, staff awareness of phishing emails and payment fraud, such as fake changes to supplier bank details.
  • Personal information: worker and client data must be protected in line with the Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA).
  • Skills: train staff so systems are used correctly.

Key points

  • A business must create customer value, stay profitable and manage cash and risk.
  • Business functions include operations, marketing, finance, HR, purchasing and quality.
  • IT supports traceability, quality, cold chain monitoring, certification and finance.
  • IT brings speed and accuracy but needs back-ups and security.
  • Personal information must be protected under POPIA.
